strengths: Clear and well-motivated framework: FSP directly targets the teacher-forcing and short-horizon limitations of NTP and MTP by predicting a compact summary of the long-term future.

Two complementary variants are proposed and analyzed: handcrafted multi-hot bag-of-words summaries (FSP-BCE) and learned reverse-LM summaries (FSP-RevLM), with controlled synthetic experiments illustrating when each is beneficial.

The paper reports large-scale pretraining experiments at 3B and 8B parameters with multiple baselines (NTP, MTP, DeepSeek-MTP) across several reasoning/code benchmarks, which is rare and valuable in this literature.

The synthetic path-star and sibling-discovery analyses provide useful conceptual evidence that long-range summaries help planning and that adaptive summaries can outperform handcrafted summaries when future information is noisy.
Ablations include different future-window lengths, random-token summaries, tf-idf reweighting, and reverse-LM depth, giving some insight into design choices.
weaknesses: The main comparison is not iso-compute: FSP-RevLM requires training an additional reverse language model of the same scale on the same data, but this teacher cost is explicitly excluded. This roughly doubles training compute relative to NTP/MTP and undermines claims of efficiency or fair comparison.

Real-world results are mixed and modest. At 8B, FSP-RevLM loses to NTP on GSM8K, ties MTP on HumanEval+, and its gains over MTP are often small. At 3B, DS-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on most tasks except math reasoning. The claim of substantial improvements is stronger than the evidence.

Baseline tuning and selection are questionable. MTP and DS-MTP are constrained to a single auxiliary head, whereas standard MTP can use multiple heads and may be stronger. DS-MTP is anomalously poor on ARC at 8B compared with 3B and with NTP, suggesting possible tuning issues. No empirical comparison is provided to related future-aware methods such as TRELAWNEY, register-token MTP, L-MTP, BST, or MiM.

Evaluation metrics are non-standard and potentially inflated: the paper reports pass@16 for code/math tasks and selects the best temperature per method and task, rather than reporting pass@1 or fixed-decoding results. This makes comparisons harder to interpret and can overstate differences.

Despite motivating FSP by long-form generation, planning, and creative writing, the paper provides no direct evaluation on long-form generation or creative-writing tasks. The real-world evaluations are limited to short reasoning and code benchmarks.

Theoretical justification for FSP-RevLM is limited. It is unclear why matching a reverse-LM hidden state is an optimal or robust future summary, what information it retains versus discards, and how sensitive performance is to the auxiliary loss weight or exact target layer/position. Some equations and target-alignment details are also underspecified.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or model release is mentioned, the pretraining data mixture is only partially specified, and the large-scale compute setup is difficult to replicate. Data licensing/consent issues for GitHub and StackExchange sources are not discussed.

strengths: Ambitious large-scale pretraining experiments at 3B and 8B parameters, with 250B and 1T tokens respectively, across multiple reasoning and coding benchmarks; this scale of comparison is costly and relatively rare.
The paper is clearly motivated, identifying limitations of NTP and MTP for long-horizon reasoning and planning, and the proposed FSP framework is conceptually simple and easy to understand.

Introduces two variants, FSP-BCE (handcrafted bag-of-words future summary) and FSP-RevLM (learned summary from a reverse language model), and provides synthetic task analyses on path-star and sibling discovery.
FSP-RevLM shows some improvements at the 8B scale, especially on ARC and MATH, and the paper reports scaling comparisons between 3B and 8B models.
Reproducibility details are partially provided, including data mixture sources, model sizes, batch sizes, sequence lengths, and training steps.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is not compute-matched. FSP-RevLM requires training an additional reverse language model, roughly doubling pretraining compute, but the paper explicitly excludes this cost and compares under iso-data conditions only. No NTP or MTP baseline is trained with equivalent extra compute, so the reported gains may simply reflect additional compute rather than a better objective.

The MTP and DS-MTP baselines are artificially weak: both are constrained to a single auxiliary head predicting only the immediate future token, whereas standard MTP and DeepSeek-MTP typically use multiple future tokens. This makes the comparison against MTP misleading, and no multiple-head MTP baseline is evaluated at scale.

Evaluation methodology has a serious flaw: for pass@k, the authors select the temperature that yields the best performance for each method and task on the test benchmarks. This test-set oracle tuning inflates scores and can bias results toward methods with higher output diversity, such as FSP-RevLM, invalidating the comparisons.

Results are mixed and often not statistically convincing. At 3B, DS-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on most benchmarks except math. At 8B, FSP-RevLM is worse than NTP on GSM8K and ties MTP on HumanEval+. Several gains are small with overlapping standard errors, and DS-MTP performs anomalously poorly at 8B on ARC without explanation.

The main claims are stronger than the evidence. The introduction claims substantial gains of up to 5% on math and coding, but the gains are inconsistent across tasks and scales, and no long-form generation or creative-writing experiments are provided despite those being the stated motivation.

The synthetic path-star analysis may be confounded: FSP-BCE predicts a bag-of-words summary of all future path nodes, which in a unique-path graph may nearly reveal the target set and allow the model to reconstruct the path from the adjacency list. No control experiment rules out label leakage or a fundamentally easier auxiliary task.

The sibling discovery analysis only reports convergence speed relative to NTP; all methods eventually produce coherent sequences, and MTP is not compared. This is weak evidence for the claimed benefit of adaptive future summaries.

Novelty is limited. FSP-RevLM is essentially knowledge distillation or representation alignment from a reverse language model, closely related to bidirectional training methods such as BST and Meet-in-the-Middle. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish its contribution or compare against these methods at scale.

The theoretical justification that FSP reduces teacher forcing is informal and unmeasured. The learned summary may force the forward model to match future information that is not predictable from the prefix, potentially injecting noise, and no analysis of what information the reverse-LM hidden state actually captures is provided.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or model release is mentioned, exact data mixture proportions are omitted, optimizer and warmup details are missing, and reverse-LM training details are sparse. The pass@16 evaluation with per-method best temperature is also non-standard and hard to reproduce faithfully.

Related work positioning is insufficient. The paper does not compare at scale against recent lookahead or future-prediction methods such as TRELAWNEY, register-token prediction, or other leap-based MTP variants, despite citing them.

strengths: Proposes Future Summary Prediction (FSP), a well-motivated auxiliary pretraining objective that predicts a compact summary of the long-term future rather than individual future tokens, with two concrete variants: handcrafted multi-hot BCE summaries and learned reverse-LM summaries.
Conducts large-scale pretraining experiments at 3B and 8B parameter scales on 250B and 1T tokens, which is rare in the literature and provides valuable empirical evidence.
Combines controlled synthetic analyses (path-star graph, sibling discovery) with real-world benchmark evaluations, giving insight into when long-range and adaptive future summaries help.
FSP-RevLM shows clear improvements over NTP and MTP on several 8B-scale benchmarks, notably ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MATH, and MBPP.
The paper is generally well written, with clear motivation, helpful diagrams, and useful ablations on summary window size, tf-idf reweighting, and reverse-LM depth.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not compute-fair: FSP-RevLM requires training a separate reverse language model, but this teacher-training cost is excluded from the reported compute budget. Baselines such as NTP, MTP, and DS-MTP do not receive equivalent extra compute, so the observed gains may be due to additional training rather than the proposed objective.

There is no reported decontamination of the pretraining corpus against the evaluation benchmarks (MATH, GSM8K, ARC, MBPP, HumanEval+), despite the corpus including math and reasoning datasets. This raises serious concerns that some gains may reflect benchmark contamination or memorization.

For pass@k evaluation, the authors select the best temperature per method and task on the test set. This is a non-standard, test-set-tuned protocol that can inflate results, especially for a method like FSP-RevLM that is explicitly claimed to increase output diversity.

The DS-MTP baseline at 8B collapses on ARC (e.g., 0.617 vs. 0.718 for NTP), which is anomalous and suggests an implementation or optimization issue. The baseline is also constrained to a single auxiliary head, so it is not a faithful reproduction of DeepSeek-MTP.

The empirical story is mixed and somewhat overclaimed: FSP-RevLM underperforms NTP on 8B GSM8K, ties MTP on HumanEval+, and yields only small coding gains, yet the abstract/introduction claim broad improvements across math, reasoning, and coding.

Novelty is moderate relative to prior work on bidirectional training, belief-state models, and future-aware objectives (e.g., BST, MiM, TRELAWNEY, register-token MTP). The learned summary via reverse-LM distillation is conceptually close to existing self-distillation and bidirectional alignment methods, and these baselines are discussed but not empirically compared.

The sibling-discovery analysis lacks a standard MTP baseline and relies on a convergence-speed metric with large error bars, which weakens the claim that learned summaries are specifically necessary beyond MTP.

Several technical details are unclear: whether the reverse LM is frozen during forward-model training, how hidden-state targets are normalized/scaled, how convergence is defined in the sibling-discovery experiments, and whether any decontamination or benchmark-overlap checks were performed.

strengths: Introduces a unified future-summary prediction framework and two concrete variants, FSP-BoW and FSP-RevLM, with a clear conceptual comparison to NTP and MTP.
Provides controlled synthetic analyses on path-star and sibling discovery tasks that give useful insight into when long-range and adaptive future summaries matter.
Conducts large-scale pretraining experiments at 3B and 8B scales, which is rare and computationally valuable for the community.
Includes data-constrained pretraining experiments, showing that future-aware objectives can outperform NTP when unique data are limited.
The paper is generally well written, with good related-work coverage and an interesting preliminary interpretability analysis of the reverse LM.
The learned-summary approach is well motivated and shows some gains on math/reasoning benchmarks at the 8B scale.
weaknesses: FSP-RevLM roughly doubles training compute because the reverse LM is trained separately at the same scale. No iso-compute comparison is provided, so the reported gains may stem from extra compute/distillation rather than the FSP objective itself.
The evaluation selects the best decoding temperature and pass@k per method and task on the test set, which is non-standard and can overfit the benchmark, making comparisons unreliable.

The central claim of consistent improvements over both NTP and MTP across math, reasoning, and coding is overstated. At 3B, DS-MTP is stronger on most tasks; at 8B, FSP-RevLM loses to NTP on GSM8K, ties MTP on HumanEval+, and several reported differences are small.
MTP and DS-MTP are constrained to a single auxiliary head, which under-represents standard MTP and does not fairly test MTP's multi-token design at scale.
Several relevant baselines are missing, including multi-head MTP, SemFormer, Next-latent prediction, and Twin Networks, despite being closely related.

Novelty is limited: FSP-BoW is close to prior bag-of-words/set-level future prediction, and FSP-RevLM is conceptually related to Twin Networks/BST; the main advance is scaling, which is confounded by compute.

Key implementation details of the reverse LM alignment are insufficient for reproducibility, including which hidden layer is used, whether the reverse model is frozen or jointly trained, and exactly how the target summary is extracted. No code or models are released.
The teacher-forcing reduction argument is informal and not directly measured; the synthetic experiments only partially validate the proposed mechanism.
Data-constrained results are also confounded by extra compute for FSP-RevLM, and they show all future-aware objectives outperform NTP, so they do not isolate a specific benefit of FSP-RevLM.
No ablation on reverse-model size/cost or comparison to training NTP longer with the same compute is provided, which is the key missing control for the central claim.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving pretraining objectives beyond standard next-token and multi-token prediction for long-horizon reasoning and planning.
It reports large-scale pretraining experiments at 3B and 8B parameter scales, which is computationally expensive and relatively rare in the literature.
The synthetic path-star and sibling-discovery analyses provide useful intuition about when long future summaries may help and when adaptive learned summaries may be necessary.
The data-constrained pretraining experiments are a relevant addition, suggesting future-aware objectives can outperform NTP when unique data are limited.
The proposed FSP framework is simple and can be integrated with existing MTP-style auxiliary heads.
weaknesses: Major compute confound: FSP-RevLM trains a same-size reverse language model for the same number of steps, roughly doubling training compute, yet this cost is excluded from comparisons. No iso-compute baselines (e.g., NTP/MTP trained with 2x compute or a larger model) are provided, so the central claim that the objective itself drives the gains is unsupported.

Baselines are weakened: MTP and DS-MTP are constrained to a single auxiliary head predicting the immediate future token, whereas standard MTP/DS-MTP often use multiple heads. Synthetic results show multiple MTP heads substantially improve performance, making the real-data comparison against MTP unconvincing.

Limited novelty: handcrafted bag-of-words/set-level future summaries and reverse-LM hidden-state alignment are closely related to prior work such as SemFormer, Twin Networks, MiM, BST, and next-latent prediction. The paper acknowledges some overlap but does not sufficiently isolate what is new or ablate key design choices.

Mixed and weak empirical results: improvements are inconsistent across tasks and scales. FSP-RevLM loses to NTP on GSM8K at 8B, is outperformed by DS-MTP on most 3B tasks, and many reported gains are within or near one standard error over only 3 seeds. The claimed 'up to 5%' gains are not consistently supported.

The learned summary via reverse LM is not well justified or specified: matching hidden states of separately trained models with an L2 loss raises representation-alignment concerns, and it is unclear whether the reverse model is frozen or co-trained, how target positions are selected, and why hidden-state matching should be meaningful across independently initialized networks.

Synthetic tasks are toy and may not support the broad conclusions. In path-star, FSP-BoW effectively supplies the unordered set of future path nodes, which may make the task easier for reasons unrelated to long-horizon planning rather than demonstrating genuine planning ability.

Missing ablations and controls: there is no comparison to a forward-order learned summary, no control for extra parameters/compute, no ablation of reverse-order versus forward-order supervision, and no iso-compute comparison in the data-constrained regime. The data-constrained analysis still confounds compute with objective.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or model release is mentioned, and key implementation details of reverse LM training, target selection, gradient flow, and hidden-state alignment are incomplete. The reference list and writing also contain errors and typos, reducing clarity.

Significance is overstated: the method is an auxiliary-target variant of MTP rather than a fundamentally 'beyond MTP' framework, and the practical gains are modest relative to the doubled training compute and added complexity.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of next-token and multi-token prediction for long-horizon reasoning by proposing future summary prediction, a conceptually simple and well-motivated auxiliary objective.

It introduces two concrete variants, handcrafted bag-of-words summaries and learned reverse-LM summaries, and places them in a broader framework that helps explain when long-range versus adaptive future supervision is useful.

The synthetic path-star and sibling-discovery analyses are well chosen and provide controlled evidence for the key conceptual claims, including useful negative results such as MTP with more heads still failing on longer paths and random future tokens hurting performance.
The paper reports large-scale pretraining experiments at 3B and 8B parameters, with 250B and 1T tokens, multiple baselines, and three seeds, which is rare and valuable for this line of work.
The ablation suite is broad, covering future-window length, tf-idf reweighting, RevLM depth, data-constrained pretraining, language-modeling metrics, and output diversity.
The writing is generally clear and the method and motivation are easy to follow.
weaknesses: The main real-world comparisons are not iso-compute. FSP-RevLM trains an additional same-size reverse language model for the same number of steps, roughly doubling total compute, while NTP/MTP baselines receive no equivalent extra compute. Excluding the teacher cost is not sufficient here because the reverse model is trained from scratch on the same data, so the central claim that FSP is a better pretraining objective than NTP/MTP is confounded by extra compute. Compute-matched baselines are needed.

The evaluation protocol tunes decoding temperature on the test set by reporting the temperature that yields the best pass@k for each method and task. This is an invalid comparison practice, can overfit benchmarks, and may inflate the apparent diversity and pass@k gains of FSP-RevLM.

The gains are modest and inconsistent. At 8B scale FSP-RevLM loses to NTP on GSM8K, the MATH improvement is small and within noise, and several differences have overlapping standard errors. At 3B scale DS-MTP is stronger on most tasks. The claim that FSP scales more favorably is based on only two model sizes with different architectures and token budgets, not a controlled scaling study.

Novelty is incremental. Future-summary prediction, reverse-LM training, and forward-reverse alignment have close relatives in prior work such as Twin Networks, BST, SemFormer, ProphetNet, MiM, and other future-aware objectives. The paper acknowledges these but does not empirically compare against them, so it is unclear whether the proposed method is better than existing future-aware or planning objectives at scale.

The introduction motivates long-form generation, planning, and creative writing, but the evaluation covers only reasoning, math, and code benchmarks plus small synthetic graph tasks. There is no direct evaluation of long-form generation or narrative coherence, so the central motivation is not fully tested.

MTP and DS-MTP baselines are restricted to a single auxiliary head predicting the immediate future token. Although this is done for consistency, it may under-represent stronger MTP configurations, and the 'beyond MTP' claim would be more convincing with standard or compute-matched MTP variants.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. The auxiliary-head architecture, the weighting between NTP and FSP losses, whether the reverse LM is frozen during FSP training, and the exact data mixture are not fully specified. The 8B pretraining is also unlikely to be reproducible by most reviewers.
The claim that FSP reduces teacher forcing is intuitive but not formally measured. A quantitative diagnostic or controlled metric beyond the synthetic tasks would strengthen the argument.

FSP-BoW introduces a vocabulary-sized binary classification head at every position, which may be computationally expensive, but the paper does not analyze the parameter or compute overhead of the auxiliary heads relative to baselines.
